videos.description:
SQL injection is one of the most damaging web vulnerabilities, and SQLMap is the standard tool for testing it. In this hands-on Chapter 46, you'll learn what SQL injection is, how SQLMap detects it, how to test a practice app in your own lab, how to read the results, and most importantly how developers prevent it. All demos use an intentionally vulnerable practice app on your own VM.

⏱ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 What SQL injection is, in one picture
1:00 Why it happens
2:15 Set up a practice app (DVWA) on your VM
3:30 Your first SQLMap test in the lab
5:00 Reading the results
6:15 What the real impact looks like
7:15 How developers prevent SQL injection

📋 QUICK CHEAT SHEET
sqlmap -h: list the basic options
sqlmap -u "yourlab.local/page?id=1": test one parameter on your lab app
sqlmap -u "URL" --cookie="cookie-value": test a page that needs a login
sqlmap -u "URL" --batch: accept default answers
sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs: list databases on your lab app
Use your own practice app only, and check the SQLMap documentation for your version.

🛡 HOW DEVELOPERS PREVENT SQL INJECTION
• Use parameterized queries (prepared statements), never string-built SQL
• Use an ORM or a framework that parameterizes by default
• Validate input, but don't rely on it alone
• Give the database account only the permissions it needs
• Hide detailed database errors from users
• Keep software updated and use a web application firewall as an extra layer

🧪 SAFE PRACTICE TARGETS
• DVWA or OWASP Juice Shop, installed on your own VM
• Keep the practice app on your lab network only
• Take a VM snapshot first

⚠️ BEFORE YOU TEST ANYTHING
• Test only your own lab or sites you have written permission to test
• SQLMap sends many requests and can damage or overload a database
• Never test your school, workplace or random websites
• Report real vulnerabilities through the site's responsible-disclosure page

⚖️ LEGAL NOTE
Testing databases or websites without authorization is illegal in many places. Laws vary by country, so check your local rules.

❓ QUICK FAQ
Does SQLMap work on any website?
Only run it on systems you own or are authorized to test, and it only finds issues that exist.

What is the best defense?
Parameterized queries, plus least-privilege database accounts.

videos.title: Linux Security Audit with Lynis: Find Weak Spots in Your System Ch. 45
videos.description:
Is your Linux system secure? In this beginner-friendly Chapter 45, you'll learn what a security audit is, which areas to check (users, permissions, services, packages and open ports), how to review them with built-in commands, and how an automated tool such as Lynis can report weaknesses for you. Run audits only on your own machines or a lab you control.

▶ Full Kali Linux Course (playlist): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLYDHfwsEk0RY
▶ Previous: Chapter 44, RedHawk : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LLeM61KmYgU&list=PLYDHfwsEk0RY&index=4
▶ Next: Chapter 46 : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LDEIGs4vxNo&list=PLYDHfwsEk0RY&index=2
▶ Subscribe to EINITIAL24 ACADEMY: https://www.youtube.com/@EINITIAL24

⏱ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 What a security audit checks
0:45 Users, groups and sudo
2:15 File permissions
3:30 Running services and open ports
4:45 Packages and updates
5:45 Automated audit with Lynis
7:15 Reading the report and fixing findings

📋 QUICK CHEAT SHEET
cat /etc/passwd: list user accounts
sudo -l: show what your user can run with sudo
last: show recent logins
ss -tulpn: show listening ports and the programs behind them
systemctl list-units --type=service: list running services
apt list --upgradable: show packages that need updates
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2 /dev/null: find SUID files to review
sudo apt install lynis: install Lynis
sudo lynis audit system: run a full audit
Commands and output vary by version, so check yours.

🔍 WHAT TO LOOK FOR
• Accounts you don't recognize, or users with more sudo rights than they need
• Files that anyone can write to, and unexpected SUID files
• Services and ports you don't need
• Outdated packages
• Weak SSH and password settings
A finding is a prompt to investigate, not a verdict.

🛠 FIXING THE BASICS
• Remove or lock unused accounts
• Tighten permissions (see Chapters 16 to 18)
• Disable services you don't use
• Update packages regularly
• Take a snapshot before you change anything

⚠️ BEFORE YOU AUDIT
• Audit only systems you own or are authorized to review
• Read what a command does before you run it with sudo
• Keep reports private, because they list your weak spots

⚖️ LEGAL NOTE
Reviewing systems without authorization is illegal in many places. Laws vary by country, so check your local rules.

❓ QUICK FAQ
Is Lynis a vulnerability scanner?
It's an auditing tool. It checks configuration and hardening, and it doesn't exploit anything.

How often should I audit?
After big changes, and on a regular schedule for systems you manage.

videos.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) for Beginners: How It Works and How to Stop It Ch. 43
videos.description:
Cross-site scripting (XSS) lets an attacker run script in another user's browser, and it is still one of the most common web vulnerabilities. In this beginner-friendly Chapter 43, you'll learn what XSS is, how stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS differ, what the real impact can be, how to test for it safely in your own lab, and how developers prevent it. All demos use an intentionally vulnerable practice app on your own VM.

▶ Full Kali Linux Course (playlist): https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLYDHfwsEk0RY
▶ Previous: Chapter 42, Nikto : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hDShYE3ItWw&list=PLYDHfwsEk0RY&index=6

⏱ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 What XSS is, in one picture
0:45 Why the browser trusts the page
1:45 Reflected XSS
2:45 Stored XSS
3:45 DOM-based XSS
4:45 Real-world impact
5:45 Safe lab demo (practice app on your VM)
7:15 How developers prevent XSS

📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
• What XSS is and why it happens
• The three types: reflected, stored and DOM-based
• What an attacker can do with it, such as session theft or page defacement
• How to test for it only in a lab you control
• How to prevent it

🔍 THE THREE TYPES
• Reflected: the input is sent back in the response right away, often through a link
• Stored: the input is saved on the server and shown to every visitor
• DOM-based: the problem is in the page's own JavaScript, not in the server response

🛡 HOW DEVELOPERS PREVENT XSS
• Encode output for the place it appears (HTML, attribute, JavaScript or URL)
• Validate input, but don't rely on it alone
• Use a Content Security Policy (CSP)
• Set cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags
• Use a modern framework that escapes output by default

🧪 SAFE PRACTICE TARGETS
• DVWA or OWASP Juice Shop, installed on your own VM
• Set the practice app to listen on your lab network only
• Take a VM snapshot first

⚠️ BEFORE YOU TEST ANYTHING
• Test only your own lab or sites you have written permission to test
• Don't test your school, workplace or random websites
• Never post a working attack against a real site
• Report real vulnerabilities through the site's responsible-disclosure page

⚖️ LEGAL NOTE
Testing websites without authorization is illegal in many places. Laws vary by country, so check your local rules.

❓ QUICK FAQ
Is XSS dangerous?
Yes. It can expose sessions and data, which is why prevention matters.

What is the best defense?
Context-aware output encoding, plus a Content Security Policy.

No. It's a lead to verify.

Whois data is public, and many domains redact personal details.

It requests thousands of URLs, which servers can log and block.

🧅 ONION ROUTING IN SHORT
Your Tor client picks three relays: entry, middle and exit. It wraps your data in three layers of encryption, one for each relay. Each relay removes only its own layer, so it learns only where to pass the data next.
• The entry relay knows who you are, but not what you are visiting
• The middle relay knows neither
• The exit relay knows the destination, but not who you are

🚫 WHAT TOR CAN'T DO
• It doesn't protect you if you log in to personal accounts
• The exit relay can see unencrypted traffic, so use HTTPS sites
• Browser settings, add-ons and habits can still identify you
• An attacker who watches both ends of the connection may be able to correlate traffic
• It is slower than a normal connection
• It doesn't protect you from malware or unsafe downloads

🛡 SAFE HABITS

• Don't install extra browser add-ons

⚖️ LEGAL NOTE
Tor is legal in many countries and restricted in some, so check your local laws. This course supports lawful learning only.

❓ QUICK FAQ
Does Tor make me completely anonymous?
No. It makes tracing much harder, but your behavior can still identify you.

Why are there three relays?
So that no single relay knows both who you are and what you are visiting.

Is Tor the same as a VPN?
No. A VPN uses one provider's server, and Tor uses several relays run by volunteers.

Without a proxy: you send a request straight to the website, and the website sees your IP address.
With a proxy: you send your request to the proxy, the proxy sends it to the website on your behalf, and the website sees the proxy's IP address. The response comes back the same way.

🧰 TYPES OF PROXIES
• HTTP proxy: handles web traffic. It can read and change unencrypted web requests.
• HTTPS proxy: handles encrypted web traffic by passing it through a tunnel. The proxy can see which site you connect to, but not the encrypted content.
• SOCKS proxy (SOCKS5 is the common version): works at a lower level and can carry many kinds of traffic, not only web pages.
• Transparent, anonymous and high-anonymity proxies: they differ in whether they tell the website that a proxy is in use, and whether they pass along your real IP.

• Forward proxy: sits in front of users and sends their requests out to the internet. Used by companies, schools and privacy tools.
• Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers and receives requests on their behalf. Used for load balancing, caching, TLS termination and protection.
Same idea, opposite side of the connection.

• Privacy: hiding your IP address from the sites you visit
• Access control: companies and schools filtering or logging web traffic
• Caching: speeding up repeated requests
• Load balancing and protection: reverse proxies in front of busy websites
• Security testing: intercepting and inspecting traffic in authorized tests
• Web scraping: collecting public data, within a site's terms and the law

📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
• How to read the 10-character permission string in ls -l
• What u, g, o and a stand for
• How to add permissions with + (for example u+x)
• How to remove permissions with - (for example g-w)
• How to set exact permissions with = (for example o=r)
• How to combine several changes in one command
• How symbolic mode compares with numeric mode

📋 QUICK CHEAT SHEET
ls -l file.txt: show permissions, owner and group
chmod u+x file.txt: add execute for the owner
chmod g+w file.txt: add write for the group
chmod o-r file.txt: remove read from others
chmod a+r file.txt: add read for everyone (a means all)
chmod o=r file.txt: set others to read-only, replacing whatever they had
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r file.txt: set all three groups at once
chmod u+x,g-w file.txt: make several changes in one command
chmod -R g+r foldername: apply a change to a folder and everything inside it

🔍 HOW TO READ -RWXR-XR--
The first character is the type: a dash for a file, d for a directory. The next nine characters are three groups of three.
rwx = owner (user): read, write, execute
r-x = group: read and execute
r-- = others: read only

➕ THE THREE OPERATORS
• + adds a permission and leaves the others unchanged
• - removes a permission and leaves the others unchanged
• = sets exactly what you list and removes anything else for that group

🔁 SYMBOLIC VS NUMERIC
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r file.txt gives the same result as chmod 754 file.txt. Symbolic mode is easier to read and lets you change one permission without retyping the rest. Numeric mode is faster when you set all three groups at once. Most people use both.

⚠️ COMMON BEGINNER MISTAKES
• Using + when you meant =, and leaving old permissions in place
• Putting a space inside the mode, such as u+x, g-w with a space after the comma
• Forgetting that o means others, not owner
• Forgetting -R when changing a whole folder
• Running chmod on system files you don't understand
• Not checking the result with ls -l

🧱 REMEMBER FOLDERS
On a folder, read lets you list the contents, write lets you create and delete files inside, and execute lets you enter it with cd.

🧪 SAFE PRACTICE EXERCISE

📋 QUICK CHEAT SHEET
ls -l: show permissions, owner and group
chmod +x script.sh: make a file executable
chmod u+x script.sh: add execute for the owner only
chmod g-w file.txt: remove write from the group
chmod o=r file.txt: give others read-only access

chmod 755 script.sh: owner full access, everyone else read and execute

./script.sh: run a script in the current folder
exit: close the current shell, or leave an su session (Ctrl + D does the same)

🔢 HOW THE NUMBERS WORK
Read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1. Add them up for each group.
7 = 4 + 2 + 1 (read, write, execute)
6 = 4 + 2 (read, write)
5 = 4 + 1 (read, execute)

🧱 PERMISSIONS ON FOLDERS
On a folder, read lets you list its contents, write lets you create and delete files inside it, and execute lets you enter it with cd.

A virtual machine runs a second operating system inside your current one. If something breaks, you delete it and start again, and your main computer stays safe. 🌐 NETWORK MODES AT A GLANCE
• NAT: the VM reaches the internet through your computer, and it's hidden from your local network. The safest default for beginners.
• Bridged: the VM appears as a separate device on your network. Useful for lab scenarios, but more exposed.
• Host-Only: the VM can talk only to your computer, with no internet. Good for isolated testing.
• NAT Network: lets several VMs talk to each other and the internet. Handy for multi-machine labs later in the course.

⚙️ SETTINGS CHECKLIST BEFORE CREATING A VM
• Make sure virtualization (Intel VT-x or AMD-V) is turned on in your BIOS or UEFI settings
• Give the VM enough RAM, but leave enough for your main system (more RAM means a smoother VM)
• Assign at least 2 CPU cores if your computer allows it
• Allow enough disk space for the OS and tools
• Pick your network mode (see above)

🛠 COMMON PROBLEMS
• "VT-x is not available" or the VM won't start: enable virtualization in BIOS or UEFI, and check for conflicts with Hyper-V or other Windows virtualization features
• The VM is slow: increase RAM and CPU cores, and close heavy apps on your main system
• Kernel driver errors on Linux hosts: install your distribution's kernel headers and build tools, then reinstall
• Apple Silicon Macs: VirtualBox works differently on ARM Macs, so check the official VirtualBox documentation for what is supported
• Always download from the official site, and use the version listed there for your system

🕰 UNIX IN A NUTSHELL
Unix was created at Bell Labs in 1969 by Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie and others. It became the foundation for many commercial operating systems, such as AIX, HP-UX and Solaris, and macOS is also a certified Unix system. Unix is typically proprietary, and the name "UNIX" is a certification managed by The Open Group.

🐧 LINUX IN A NUTSHELL
Linux started in 1991 as a hobby kernel written by Linus Torvalds. It was written from scratch and follows Unix design ideas, which is why it's called "Unix-like." Combined with tools from the GNU project, it became the free and open-source operating system that now runs servers, phones (Android), cloud infrastructure and most security tools.

⚔️ UNIX VS LINUX: QUICK COMPARISON
• Origin: Unix came from Bell Labs in 1969. Linux came from Linus Torvalds in 1991.
• Source code: Linux is not derived from the original Unix source code.
• License: Linux is free and open source. Many Unix systems are proprietary.
• Cost: Linux is free. Commercial Unix often requires a license.
• Hardware: Linux runs on almost anything. Traditional Unix often ran on specific vendor hardware.
• Usage today: Linux dominates servers, cloud and security work.

🐉 WHERE DOES KALI LINUX FIT IN?
Kali Linux is a Debian-based Linux distribution built for penetration testing and security research. Because it's Linux, it follows the same Unix-style philosophy: everything is a file, you work through a powerful command line, and small tools can be combined. Understanding this makes the file system, terminal and commands in the next chapters much easier.

🧠 WHY THIS MATTERS FOR CYBERSECURITY
Most servers and network devices you'll test as an ethical hacker run Linux or Unix-like systems. Knowing how they work helps you understand permissions, processes, file systems and logs, which is the base of every security skill.

❌ COMMON MYTHS
• "Linux is Unix." It's Unix-like, but not Unix.
• "Unix is dead." It's still used in enterprise and legacy systems.
• "Linux is only for hackers." It runs most of the internet.
• "Kali Linux is a different OS from Linux." It's a Linux distribution.
